**Abstract**

Biodiversity is under pressure from multiple global change drivers including climate change, pollution, and land-use change. Theory suggests that several of these drivers affect plant diversity through their impacts on plant community biomass. We hypothesize that by using community biomass as a common currency, we can arrive at a more synthetic understanding of the direct and indirect effects of multiple global change drivers on plant diversity. We test this prediction in a replicated field experiment in alpine and sub-alpine grasslands, simulating the effects of climate warming, nitrogen addition, and grazing. Our study showed that the three global change drivers operated indeed on diversity through community biomass, but the response was stronger in the temperature and nutrient limited alpine site. At the warmer sub-alpine site, the direct effects of warming and nitrogen addition can override the biomass-mediated effects. Using environmental affinities to describe the change in environmental niches of the plant communities revealed a useful approach to understand the underlying mechanisms.

**Keywords:** adaptive management, biodiversity, climate change, productivity, land-use change, mountains, pollution

## Introduction

Anthropogenic global changes such as land-use change, resource exploitation, climate change, invasive alien species, and pollution pose major and accelerating threats to biodiversity and ecosystem functioning [@Ipbes2019-sd]. These global change drivers do not act in isolation but occur simultaneously and often interact in complex ways so that their cumulative impacts may exceed the sum of single drivers [@oliver2014interactions; @Komatsu2019-yr; @rillig2019role; @Speiser2022-st; @xue2024number; @fig-concept a]. Given these complexities, forecasting changes to biodiversity require an understanding of the mechanisms underlying the multifactorial and interactive nature of anthropogenic global change drivers.

A growing body of literature suggests that different global change drivers can affect community biomass, plant community diversity and composition in grasslands, through a similar underlying mechanisms; changes in community biomass that shift the intensity and nature of the dominant plant-plant interactions and result in increased competitive exclusion [@borer2014herbivores; @li2024water; @harpole2016addition; @klein2004experimental; @collins2022global]. For example, warming and nitrogen addition typically increase community biomass (@fig-concept b), which may lead to communities with taller, faster growing species that are stronger competitors [@Alexander2015-gu; @Vandvik2020-hu; @wust2021interaction]. A few studies have explicitly shown that this increased competition is for light [@eskelinen2022light; @hautier2009competition]. In contrast, grazing removes biomass [@frank2005interactive; @Bernes2015-yg], which can lead to increased diversity, particularly in more productive habitats [@Austrheim2001-nu; @frank2005interactive; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @borer2024planning; @proulx1998reversal]. Accordingly, grazing has been shown in some cases to reverse the effects of warming and nitrogen addition, thus preventing species loss [@kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @klein2004experimental; @borer2014herbivores; @post2008opposing; @song2020g].

While these studies suggest that different global change drivers can modify the magnitude and nature of competition for resources, the hypothesis that their combined impacts are mediated through the same mechanism – i.e., changes in community biomass – has rarely been tested in a unified way. @white2014direct studied direct and indirect effects of different drivers on plant diversity in three temperate grasslands and identified shoot biomass as a key indirect driver of species loss in response to grazing and precipitation. @Vandvik2020-hu showed that complex interactions of temperature and precipitation change could be simplified by including the biomass of novel species as a proxy of plant-plant interactions. Building on these findings, we propose that we can synthesize the effects of multiple global change drivers on plant biodiversity more generally by using community biomass as a *common currency*, integrating the underlying impacts of these drivers on the intensity and outcome of plant-plant interactions for limiting resources (@fig-concept a and b). This would imply that knowing the general patterns and trends in community biomass could be used to predict the changes in plant biodiversity, without having to identify and test the direct effects of all the different global change drivers on specific mechanisms in each specific case. Furthermore, the magnitude of change in community biomass can serve as a proxy for the intensity of the effect of these global change drivers on biodiversity.

![Two alternative hypotheses for how three global change drivers climate warming, nitrogen addition, and biomass removal via clipping or grazing affect plant diversity. a) Warming, nitrogen deposition, and clipping (or grazing) affect diversity directly, or b) these drivers affect diversity indirectly, via their impacts on biotic interactions such as competition for light or nutrients, mediated through community biomass as a *common currency*.](figures/Figure1_hypotheses.png){#fig-concept width="600"}

We hypothesize that climate warming, nitrogen addition, and grazing affect diversity and species composition via impacts on community biomass. Specifically, we expect warming and nitrogen addition to increase community biomass, leading to an increase in the intensity of competition for light and nutrients and an increase in competitive exclusion. Grazing should have the opposite effects. Alternative mechanisms are also possible. For example, some species may be physiologically intolerant of very high or low temperature and therefore go locally extinct or successfully colonise with changing temperature, regardless of the competitive environment [@nomoto2021drivers]. Second, increased nitrogen addition, especially at high levels, can lead to acidic soil conditions [@tian2015global], which can lead to shifts in species composition and diversity due to differences in tolerance to acidic conditions, independently of competitive interactions. Similarly, some species may be particularly tolerant or intolerant to direct effects of grazing irrespective of competitive interactions [@archibald2019unified]. Such shifts in species composition might therefore not be mediated through community biomass. We use ecological indicators of responses to the environmental conditions [@diekmann2003species; @rumpf2018range] to describe species community composition and can provide further insights into the mechanisms of these dynamics.

To test the generality of this mechanism, we conduct experiments in mountain grasslands replicated along an elevational gradient (@fig-methods). Mountains harbor unique biodiversity and are subjected to multiple global change drivers [@dainese2024global; @Humbert2016-wg; @verrall2020alpine; @Ipbes2019-sd]. In addition, plant community responses to global change drivers often vary along environmental gradients and across habitats thus making elevational gradients an ideal natural laboratory to study global change impacts [@milchunas1993quantitative; @elmendorf2012plot; @Humbert2016-wg; @bjorkman2018plant; @delnevo2018plastic; @Vandvik2020-hu; @tito2020mountain]. We therefore manipulate three common global change drivers in a field experiment: climate warming, nitrogen deposition, and clipping or natural grazing, replicated in an alpine and sub-alpine grassland community in Western Norway (@fig-methods). Plant communities were transplanted to lower elevation to simulate warmer climate. We fertilised the communities using seven levels of nitrogen, ranging between 0 and 100 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^, and simulated grazing by clipping at two different intensities and had one natural grazing treatment. After three years of global change treatments, we harvested community biomass at peak growing season and assessed the change in vascular plant species composition and diversity.
